title: Doubles and Near Doubles
child_idea: A double is two of the same number added. If two numbers are next to each other, use a double and then add 1 or take away 1.

topics: Mental addition within 20 using doubles (1 + 1 to 10 + 10)
Near doubles as a mental strategy (7 + 8 is double 7 and 1 more)
Adding more than two numbers (Go further only)
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. FLAGGED NEW TOPIC: the plan marks this lesson as a new topic that needs an owner or tutor syllabus check before it is used with children (not yet done). Doubles to 10 + 10, tens doubles (30 + 30) and 'a double and 1 more' sit within the school Primary 1 idea of adding within 20 and 100. Beyond Primary 1 on purpose and only at Go further: doubling a two-digit number that is not a tens number (double 35, which needs renaming) and adding five numbers that are almost the same. Say this plainly to families. Do not describe the lesson as MOE-aligned or syllabus-aligned. Every Start here item is reached with ten-frames, dominoes or tens bars and counters after Explore.

contest_moves: double and adjust by one (near doubles)
find the middle number of several almost-equal numbers
objectives: Say and write the double of any number from 1 to 10 (4 + 4 = 8, double 7 is 14) using counters, ten-frames or a domino, and the double of a tens number (3 tens and 3 tens make 6 tens).
Add two numbers that are next to each other (7 + 8, 8 + 9) by using a double and then 1 more or 1 less, and say why the answer is 1 away from the double.
Choose which double to use for a near double (7 + 8 is double 7 and 1 more, or double 8 and 1 less) and spot when two numbers are not next to each other.
Go further: add numbers that are almost the same (8 + 9 + 8 + 7 + 8) by thinking of the number in the middle.

remember: How many more make 10 on a ten-frame, shown with fingers (7 needs 3)
Tens add: 3 tens and 3 tens make 6 tens (counted with tens bars)
Same amount on both sides: 5 + 3 = 4 + 4 (move 1 counter from one plate to the other)
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20 and ten ones making a ten. Nothing from an earlier lesson is needed: the warm-up builds a ten-frame, tens bars and two plates with counters, and the double idea itself is taught in Explore with objects.
joining_cold.note: Lesson 13 is fairly safe to miss: it stands alone after the warm-up. A child who misses it watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2 before Lesson 14. Doubles help later (Lesson 16 uses the 2 table), but nothing in Lessons 14 or 15 needs them.

child: The printed workbook and the kit page (page 6), with the 20 counters (10 red, 10 yellow) cut out by a grown-up beforehand
If no printer is available: about 20 small things of two kinds (for example 10 buttons and 10 coins)
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
Optional: a clean empty egg carton (a double of 6) and a set of dominoes
tutor: A slide deck and a paper copy of the kit page with red and yellow counters to show on camera if you wish
kit_pages: Four ten-frames and 20 counters (10 red, 10 yellow), printed on page 6 of the workbook. The counters are cut out before the lesson. This lesson uses up to 10 red and 10 yellow counters at a time
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought: everything can be found at home. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Small things never go near the mouth or ears.

timing.notes: Opening is 2 minutes (the routine and rules were taught earlier in the term; give the recording, muting and camera notice). Explore has 15 minutes because the lesson is hands-on and the mini-lesson has 11 because it carries three worked examples (near doubles, next to each other, almost the same). The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.
skip_order: Start with: shorten Explore round 3 to one build (7 + 8)
Then: shorten the Mini-lesson check slide to two questions
Then: take the extra minutes from the flex time

sneak_peek.q1: Mei puts 4 red counters in one frame and 4 yellow counters in another frame. How many counters are there altogether? You may draw to help.
sneak_peek.q2: Ben knows that 6 + 6 = 12. He says that 6 + 7 is 1 more than 12. Is Ben right? Circle Yes or No. Then write or draw how you know.
sneak_peek.a2: Yes. 6 + 7 is 6 + 6 with one more counter, so 12 + 1 = 13.

opening.say: If you are watching the recording: hello! Get a pencil, paper, your workbook, your kit page and counters. Pause or rewind any time.
opening.action: Gather your workbook, pencil, paper, kit pieces and small things. Press play when ready.

remember.say: Recording: join in! Show your answers on your fingers before I say them. Pause if you need longer.
remember.action: Play along. Show each answer on your fingers before the video does.

sneak.say: Recording: pause now and try both puzzles on your paper. Guessing is fine. Press play for the next part.
sneak.action: Pause. Try both puzzles on your own paper. A guess is fine.

break.say: Recording: stand up and join in! Stomp and clap each double with me.
break.action: Stand up. Stomp the number on each foot and say the double.

talk.say: Recording: pause. Tell a grown-up who is right, and show them with counters.
talk.action: Pause. Explain your answer to someone at home, with counters and a reason.

exit.say: Recording: pause and do the exit ticket on your own. Then press play to check it.
exit.action: Pause. Do the exit ticket alone, then play to check it.

look.say: Recording: pause and fill in your look-back box. You can pass.
look.action: Pause. Fill in the look-back box, or pass.

flex.say: Recording: well done for finishing! Show a grown-up one thing you found out.
flex.action: Show a grown-up your workbook and tell them one thing you found out.

explore.say: Recording: pause now. Build the doubles with red and yellow counters, then try one more and one less. Press play when you have tried.
explore.action: Pause. Build each double with red and yellow counters. Then add 1 more and take 1 away. Say each total.

mini.say: Recording: keep watching and copy the examples. Rewind if you miss a step.
mini.action: Watch and copy the examples. Rewind any step you missed.

work.say: Recording: pause now and do workbook page 1. When you finish a page, press play to check it.
work.action: Pause. Do page 1, then play to check. Then page 2. Then choose a page to try.

lines.text: @rec

Hello, inquirers! Please stay muted unless I invite you to speak. Cameras on if you can, so I can see your page and hands; cameras off is fine too. Pencil ready, and your counters, the kit page and your workbook on the table.
This lesson is recorded so a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted. You may mute and keep your camera off.
Today we learn about doubles: two of the same number. Then we use a double to add numbers that are next to each other.
If you can, greet each child by first name before you start the recording. While it runs, avoid names. Check that the page and hands can be seen, or ask the grown-up.

Say the recording notice in the SAY line above in your own words: the recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any unmuted voice; children may mute and keep the camera off. The routine and the four inquirer rules were introduced earlier in the term: do not re-teach them.

New here? Say in one minute: our three rule words (notice it, test it, explain why); a guess is fine and you can always pass; after Start here you may choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody holds paper to the camera. The first recording of the term shows the full routine.
@rec
Fingers and a ten-frame. A ten-frame has ten spaces. I say how many counters are in the frame. You show me, on your fingers, how many more fill it up.
Seven counters. How many more to make ten?
Four counters. How many more to make ten?
Nine counters. How many more?
Six counters. How many more?
Now tens. A tens bar is a ten. Three tens and three tens. Count the bars, then say the number.
Three tens and three tens. How many tens, and what is the number?
Two tens and two tens. What number?
Four tens and four tens. What number?
Last one. Two plates. Move one counter from the left plate to the right plate. Nothing is added and nothing is lost, so both sides stay equal. Five and three is the same as four and four.
Six and two is the same as five and what?
Seven and one is the same as six and what?
Five and three is the same as four and what?

If a child hesitates on how many more make ten, count the empty spaces in the ten-frame slowly with them. For tens, show the bars on the slide and count them in tens: ten, twenty, thirty. For the plates, move a counter on screen or on the child's own kit and count each side again.

Answers: 3, 6, 1, 4, 2 then 6 tens (60), 40, 80 then 3, 2, 4. Children answer with fingers, hands or a whispered number. Nobody writes. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20 and ten ones making a ten; the pictures do the rest.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Mei puts 4 red counters in one frame and 4 yellow counters in another frame. How many counters are there altogether? You may draw to help.
Children count the counters and write the number on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Ben knows that 6 plus 6 is 12. He says that 6 plus 7 is 1 more than 12. Is Ben right? Circle Yes or No. Then write or draw how you know.
Children write or draw their answer.
Keep your paper. Nobody shows it. We will check our own thinking later, at Talk time.

Puzzle 1 answer: 8 counters. Puzzle 2 answer: yes; 6 + 7 is the double 6 + 6 with one more counter, so 13. Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who said it is the same and one more). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today your hands are the teachers. Put the ten-frame page in front of you. Take red counters and yellow counters. Put 3 red counters in one frame and 3 yellow counters in the next frame.
How many counters altogether?
Two of the same number. We call that a double. Double 3 is 6. Say it with me: three and three is six.
Now build double 4. Four red, four yellow.
Children build 4 red and 4 yellow and count 8.
What is double 4?
Double 5.
Children build 5 red and 5 yellow: one frame is full.
What is double 5? What do you notice about the red frame?
Round two. Bigger doubles. Fill the first frame with red counters. Put the same number of yellow counters in the other frame. Then fill the first frame up to ten and say what is left.
Build double 6: 6 red, 6 yellow. Move 4 yellow into the first frame: ten and 2.
Double 6 is ten and what?
Build double 7: ten and 4.
Double 7 is ten and what? What is the number?
Build double 8: ten and 6.
Build double 9: ten and 8.
Double 8 and double 9. What are the numbers?
Round three. Build double 7 again: seven red, seven yellow. Now put one more yellow counter in the yellow frame.
Children add 1 yellow counter: 7 red and 8 yellow.
Seven and eight. How many now? How do you know?
Now take two yellow counters away from the yellow frame. That leaves six yellow.
Children take away 2 yellow counters: 7 red and 6 yellow.
Seven and six. How many? Is that more or less than double 7?
Your turn. Eight red and nine yellow.
Children build 8 and 9 (double 8, then 1 more): 17.
What did you notice? What happens to the total when the yellow counters go up by 1? What happens when they go down by 1?
A double is easy to know. If the numbers are next to each other, find the double, then move one. That is the whole trick.

A child who adds all the counters again by counting from 1: ask them to start from the red frame, which they already know is a double, and add on one yellow counter. A child who has few counters: use two kinds of small things from the table, or kit squares and pencil dots.

Main room only: no breakout rooms. Children say their totals aloud; you cannot see builds on small tiles. Answers: double 3 is 6, double 4 is 8, double 5 is 10; double 6 is 12 (10 and 2), double 7 is 14 (10 and 4), double 8 is 16, double 9 is 18; 7 + 8 is 15, 7 + 6 is 13, 8 + 9 is 17. Say the word double once as a name and use it the same way every time. Do not teach 'near double' as a rule yet: let children say it.
@rec
Look at the doubles we built. Double 1 is 2, double 2 is 4. The doubles go up by 2 each time. Read them with me up to double 10, which is 20.
Which doubles do you already know without counting?
Doubles with tens. Three tens and three tens make six tens. Thirty and thirty is sixty. A double of a tens number works the same way.
Double 2 tens? Double 4 tens? What are the numbers?
Now seven and eight. The numbers are next to each other. Find the double: double 7 is 14. The yellow frame has one more, so 14 and 1 more is 15.
How could we check 7 + 8 with a different method?
Two ways to see seven and eight. Use double 7 and add 1. Or use double 8 and take 1 away. Look at both pictures.
Which double would you choose? Does the answer change?
Not every sum is a near double. Look at the two numbers. Are they next to each other? Count from the smaller number to the larger one: is it one step?
Six and seven. Are they next to each other?
Five and eight. Are they next to each other? How many steps from 5 to 8?
Nine and ten?
Your turn. Add. Six plus seven. Eight plus nine. Four plus five. Nine plus ten.
Children write four answers.
Thirteen, seventeen, nine, nineteen. Mark your own in another colour.
One more trick. Eight, nine and seven are almost the same. The nine is one more than eight. The seven is one less than eight. They make up for each other, so it is like three eights.
What is three eights? Which number is in the middle?

Key words to use every time: double, one more, one less, next to each other. A double is two of the same number. A near double is two numbers that are next to each other. Do not say double and add 2: that is a different sum. Do not teach written column addition. Do not teach halving.

If a child gets 7 + 8 = 16, ask: which double did you use, and how many more or fewer is the second number? Count the extra yellow counter on the ten-frame picture. If a child adds 1 when they should take 1 away (8 + 9 from double 9), ask which number is the larger one.
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. I say a number. You stomp that many times with your left foot and the same with your right foot, then you say the double.
Call 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Children stomp (or tap, in a small space) both feet and say the double aloud together.
@rec

Page 1, Start here. Question 1: look at the dominoes and fill in the missing numbers. Question 2: Mei has 6 red counters and 6 yellow counters. Fill in the missing numbers. Question 3: fill in the double of 2, 5, 7 and 9.
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Question 1: six, eight, ten. Question 2: twelve, twelve. Question 3: four, ten, fourteen, eighteen. Mark your own page in another colour.
After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.

Page 2. Question 4: look at the bars and fill in the missing numbers. Question 5: Ali has 8 stickers and Ben has 8 stickers. How many stickers do they have altogether? Question 6: tick True or False for each statement.
Page 2, questions 4 to 6.
Question 4: six, sixty, eighty. Question 5: eight plus eight is sixteen; they have sixteen stickers. Question 6: true, false, true, true.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time. Anything not finished is for home too.
Stand and stretch for 30 seconds, then sit down and choose.

Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page. If Start here took the whole time, say that pages 3 to 5 are for home, and keep the time.

Q1: count the dots on one half, then the other half. Q2: count the red counters, then the yellow counters; the two frames match. Q3: use the kit counters: build the double. Q4: count the bars on one side, then say how many tens in all. Q5: draw 8 and 8, or use counters. Q6: build each double and check.

A child who is still stuck ticks 'I am still stuck' on the look-back page. The grown-up can photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp (never a personal phone). You then help in the open session in the next lesson. Never a private message to a child.

Think harder is for near doubles, which are new in this setting. Go further is mastery and extension; it goes past the school Primary 1 range on purpose (doubling 35, adding five numbers). Do not announce who is on which page. Slow class: the workbook part needs about 31 minutes against 28, so Start here may fill most of it. Take the extra minutes from the flex time, do not skip the answer slides, and say that pages 3 to 5 are for home.
@rec
Mei adds 7 plus 8. She says it is 1 more than double 7. Ali says it is 1 less than double 8. Is Mei right? Is Ali right? Use counters to show.
Build double 7 and double 8 on your frames. What happens when you move one?
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember puzzle two? Six and six is twelve. Six and seven has one more counter, so it is thirteen. Yes, Ben is right.
Did anyone change their mind about puzzle two while we worked? You can just nod.

Model answer: both are right. Double 7 is 14 and 1 more is 15. Double 8 is 16 and 1 less is 15. Both give 15. Volunteers first; never call a child by name to answer; no tallies, no rankings. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Exit ticket. Three questions, on your own, without looking back. Write your answers on page 5.
E1. Fill in the missing number. Double 9 is what? E2. Double 30 is what? E3. Add. 9 plus 8.
Children answer E1 to E3 on their own.
Eighteen. Sixty. Seventeen.
Check your own ticket in a different colour. Well done. Put a star by each one you got right.

Nothing is collected or marked live. Children tick their own ticket. If many children miss one question, spend two minutes on it at the start of the next lesson, in the open session, no names. Do not read out any child's result.
@rec

Look-back. Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. If you like, tick one thing to try next time. You can pass. Nobody reads it out. If you tick 'I am still stuck', ask your grown-up to take a photo of this page after class and send it to our business WhatsApp. Then we will help you.
Children fill in the look-back box on page 5.
Well done, inquirers. Next lesson is Odd plus Odd. Please have 20 counters or small things of one kind, a pencil and paper. Goodbye, and thank you to the grown-ups.
Optional, only if you are on time: Mei says double 9 is the same as 10 and 8. Can you see why? Build it with your counters.
Short think time, then take two answers.
Spare-time menu. If the whole class is ahead, pick one or two activities from the guide (about 4 minutes each).

This is the standing buffer. If you are behind, finish the look-back and say goodbye. Do not start anything new. Optional slide answer: double 9 is 18; move 1 counter from one 9 to the other: 10 and 8. If the whole class is ahead, use the Spare-time menu (guide section 3b) instead of rushing on.

slides.title: Doubles

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Find doubles, then use them to add.

slides.note: Lesson 3 of Term 2, 90 minutes. Objective: know the doubles to 10 + 10 and double a tens number, then add numbers that are next to each other (7 + 8) with a double and 1 more or 1 less. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 27, mini-lesson 27 to 38, brain break 38 to 42, workbook 42 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Nobody is told which page they should be on. Say the recording notice in one line: you and the screen only; a child may keep the camera off.
slides.subtitle: Doubles and Near Doubles: double, then adjust

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: fill the ten-frame

blocks.text: Show it on your fingers
A ten-frame has 10 spaces. How many more counters make 10?

slides.note: A ten-frame has ten spaces. Count the empty spaces to see how many more make ten. Say each number; children show on their fingers how many more make ten. Answers: 7 needs 3, 4 needs 6, 9 needs 1, 6 needs 4, 8 needs 2. Hands up on camera is fine. No writing, no marks. A child who is new can count the empty spaces in the picture.

slides.title: Tens and tens

blocks.text: 3 tens and 3 tens make ___ tens. That is the number ___.

items: 3 tens + 3 tens
2 tens + 2 tens
4 tens + 4 tens

slides.note: A tens bar is a ten. Three bars and three more bars make six bars: sixty. Ask each pair: three tens and three tens (6 tens, 60), two tens and two tens (4 tens, 40), four tens and four tens (8 tens, 80). Say the tens word slowly. A child who has not met tens only needs to hear and say the number words; show the bars on the slide and count them in tens.

slides.title: The same on both sides

blocks.text: Move 1 counter across. The total stays the same.

slides.note: Two plates. Moving one counter from the left plate to the right plate does not change how many counters there are, so 5 + 3 and 4 + 4 are the same total. Ask: 6 + 2 = 5 + 3 (the missing number is 3), 7 + 1 = 6 + 2 (2), then 5 + 3 = 4 + 4 (4). This is the equals-means-the-same idea that near doubles use. Show the plates picture if a child is unsure.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Mei puts 4 red counters in one frame and 4 yellow counters in another frame.
How many counters are there altogether?
You may draw to help.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Ben knows that 6 + 6 = 12.
He says that 6 + 7 is 1 more than 12.
Is Ben right? Circle Yes or No. Then write or draw how you know.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (8 counters, 4 red and 4 yellow in two ten-frames) is an access question: any child can try it by counting or drawing. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson's key idea: one more counter makes one more in the total. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper to the camera: children keep their papers and check their own thinking at Talk time. There is no private chat. Answers: 8; yes (6 + 7 is 6 + 6 and one more, so 13). Do not reveal puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list.

slides.title: Explore: build a double

items: Lay the ten-frame page in front of you.
Put 3 red counters in one frame.
Put 3 yellow counters in the other frame.
How many altogether? Then try 4 and 4, and 5 and 5.

blocks.text: Two of the same number is a double.

slides.note: Round 1, about 4 minutes. Objects first, no writing. Children put 3 red counters in one frame and 3 yellow counters in the other, then count 6. Name the idea once: two of the same number is a double, so double 3 is 6. Then double 4 (8) and double 5 (10; the red frame is full). A child without the kit page uses two kinds of small things on a drawn ten-frame, or kit squares and pencil dots.

slides.title: Bigger doubles

blocks.text: Build double 6, 7, 8 and 9. Fill the first frame up to ten. How many are left?
I move ..., so it is ten and ...

slides.note: Round 2, about 4 minutes, main room. Each child builds the double with red and yellow counters, then moves yellow counters into the first frame until it is full. The picture shows double 7: the first frame has 7 red and 3 yellow, and 4 yellow are left, so ten and 4. Answers: double 6 is 12 (ten and 2), double 7 is 14 (ten and 4), double 8 is 16 (ten and 6), double 9 is 18 (ten and 8). This links to making a ten. Do not name children.

slides.title: One more, one less

blocks.text: Build 7 + 8, then 7 + 6. Then build 8 + 9.

slides.note: Round 3, about 5 minutes. Children build double 7, add one yellow counter (7 + 8 = 15), then take two yellow away (7 + 6 = 13) so they see it is one less than the double. Then they build 8 + 9: double 8 is 16 and one more is 17. Ask: is it more or less than the double? How do you know? Children count the extra counter, not the whole frame again.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: What is double 7? What is 7 + 8?
What happens when the yellow counters go up by 1?
What happens when they go down by 1?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key ideas: a double is two of the same number; when one number goes up by 1, the total goes up by 1; when it goes down by 1, the total goes down by 1; so for numbers that are next to each other, find the double and move one. Repeat a child's answer in your own words so the recording picks it up.

slides.title: Doubles to 10 + 10
slides.note: A summary of what children built. Read the table with them: double 1 is 2, double 2 is 4, double 3 is 6, double 4 is 8, double 5 is 10, and then 12, 14, 16, 18, 20 for double 6 to 10. The totals go up by 2 each time. Ask which doubles they already know without counting; most children know 5 + 5 and 3 + 3. Take volunteers' answers and repeat them for the recording.

slides.title: Double a tens number

blocks.text: 3 tens + 3 tens = 6 tens. 30 + 30 = 60

slides.note: Double 3 is 6, so double 3 tens is 6 tens: 30 + 30 = 60. A double of a tens number works the same way as the double of a one-digit number. Ask: double 2 tens (40) and double 4 tens (80). Say the tens word slowly: forty, eighty. Beyond this slide, doubling numbers like 35 is for Go further only.

slides.title: A near double: 7 + 8

blocks.text: The numbers are next to each other: 7 and 8.

slides.note: Seven and eight are next to each other. Find the double: double 7 is 14. The yellow frame has one more counter, so add 1: 14 + 1 = 15. Ask how else to check (count on one more, or use a different double). Note that 7 + 8 is not a double itself: the numbers are different. We call a sum like this a near double. Answer: 15.

slides.title: Which double do we use?

blocks.text: Both ways: 7 + 8 = 15

slides.note: 7 + 8 can be found two ways. Use double 7 (14) and add 1, or use double 8 (16) and take 1 away. Both give 15. Ask and listen: which would you choose? Does the answer change? Do not state a rule: some children prefer the smaller double and 1 more. Answer: 15 both ways.

slides.title: Next to each other?

blocks.text: A near double has two numbers that are next to each other.

slides.note: A near double has two numbers that are next to each other, one step apart. 6 and 7: yes. 5 and 8: no, it is three steps (5, 6, 7, 8), so it is not a near double. 9 and 10: yes. Ask each pair before showing the table answers, and let children count the steps on their fingers. This prepares question T3 on page 3.

slides.title: Your turn: add

blocks.text: Write on your paper. Use a double to help.

slides.note: Each child writes four answers on their own paper. Walk the cameras. Do not ask children to hold boards up in front of the group. Some children may count on: that is fine, ask them to try a double as well. Possible doubles: 6 + 7 is double 6 and 1 (13); 8 + 9 is double 8 and 1 (17); 4 + 5 is double 4 and 1 (9); 9 + 10 is double 9 and 1 (19).

slides.title: Check: add
slides.note: Answers: 13, 17, 9, 19. Read each answer and the way we found it aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. A child who used the larger double and took one away (for example 16 - 1 for 8 + 9 is wrong, but 18 - 1 is right) can say which double they used; any correct way is fine.

slides.title: Almost the same: 8 + 9 + 7

blocks.text: The 9 is 1 more than 8. The 7 is 1 less than 8.

slides.note: A worked example for Go further. The 9 is one more than 8 and the 7 is one less than 8, so they make up for each other: the sum is three 8s, which is 24. Check: 8 + 9 = 17 and 17 + 7 = 24. Keep it to about a minute and do not rush: ask which number is in the middle. Children who are not ready can skip this idea; it is only needed for Go further.

slides.title: Stomp the double

blocks.text: I say a number. Stomp that many times on each foot.
Then say the double. Try 2, then 3, then 4.
Stand up. Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Call 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (answers 4, 6, 8, 10, 12). Children stomp that many times with the left foot, then the same with the right foot, softly, or tiptoe or tap their fingers in a small space, and say the double aloud together. No equipment.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. Take your time.

slides.note: Read questions 1 to 3 aloud. Children work on their own; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder. Question 3: children may use the ten-frame page and the red and yellow counters.

slides.title: Check page 1

start.text: Look at the dominoes. Fill in the missing numbers.
start.hint: Count the dots on one half. The other half has the same number.
start.solution: Each domino has two halves with the same number of dots. 3 + 3 = 6. 4 + 4 = 8. 5 + 5 = 10.
mistakes: Counting only one half of the domino.

start.text: Mei has 6 red counters and 6 yellow counters. Fill in the missing numbers.
start.hint: Count the red counters, then count on the yellow counters. Or fill the first frame to ten.
start.solution: The first frame has 6 red counters and the second has 6 yellow counters. 6 + 6 = 12, so double 6 is 12.

start.answer: double 2 is 4; double 5 is 10; double 7 is 14; double 9 is 18
start.hint: Use your counters or the ten-frame page. A double is two of the same number.
start.solution: Double 2 is 2 + 2 = 4. Double 5 is 5 + 5 = 10. Double 7 is 7 + 7 = 14. Double 9 is 9 + 9 = 18.

start.text: Look at the bars. Fill in the missing numbers.
start.hint: Each bar is a ten. Count the bars on both sides.
start.solution: 3 tens and 3 tens make 6 tens. 6 tens is 60. Double 4 tens is 8 tens, which is 80.

start.text: Ali has 8 stickers. Ben has 8 stickers. How many stickers do they have altogether?
start.hint: They have the same number of stickers. This is a double.
start.solution: Ali has 8 and Ben has 8. 8 + 8 = 16. They have 16 stickers altogether.

start.text: Read each statement. Decide if it is True or False.
start.hint: Work out each double first. Then decide if the statement matches.
start.solution: Double 4 is 8: True. Double 6 is 12, not 14: False. 9 + 9 is two of the same number, so it is a double: True. Double 30 is 60: True.
mistakes: Marking Double 6 is 14 as true because 6 + 6 is close to 14.
Saying 9 + 9 is not a double because 9 is a big number.

think.text: Look at the counters. Fill in the missing numbers.
think.hint: Count the red counters first. Then count on the yellow counters.
think.solution: The red frame is double 7 with the yellow: 7 + 7 = 14. The second frame has 8 yellow counters, one more than 7, so 7 + 8 = 14 + 1 = 15.

think.hint: Find the double of the smaller number. Then move one.
think.solution: 6 + 7: double 6 is 12, and 1 more is 13. 8 + 9: double 8 is 16, and 1 more is 17. 4 + 5: double 4 is 8, and 1 more is 9. 9 + 10: double 9 is 18, and 1 more is 19.
mistakes: Taking 1 away instead of adding 1 after the smaller double.

think.text: Which sum is not a near double? Write the number in the bracket.
think.hint: A near double has two numbers that are next to each other. Look at each pair.
think.solution: 6 and 7 are next to each other. 8 and 9 are next to each other. 9 and 10 are next to each other. 5 and 8 are not next to each other (they are 3 apart), so 5 + 8 is not a near double.
mistakes: Looking at the total instead of the two numbers.

think.text: Kumar adds 8 + 9. Step 1: 8 + 8 = 16. Step 2: 16 - 1 = 15. Check Step 2. Answer (a) and (b).

parts.text: Is Kumar correct? Circle Yes or No.

think.hint: The second number is greater than 8. Is the total more or less than the double?
think.solution: 9 is 1 more than 8, so the total is 1 more than 16: 16 + 1 = 17. Kumar took 1 away instead of adding 1.
mistakes: Saying Yes because 16 - 1 looks like a good step.

go.text: Add 8 + 9 + 8 + 7 + 8. Show your working on the lines.
go.hint: Look at the 9 and the 7. How far is each from 8?
go.solution: The 9 is 1 more than 8 and the 7 is 1 less than 8, so they make up for each other. The five numbers are the same as five 8s: 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 40. Another way: 8 + 8 = 16, 9 + 7 = 16, and 16 + 16 + 8 = 40.
mistakes: Adding from left to right and slipping.

go.text: Ben says 9 + 10 + 11 is the same as 10 + 10 + 10. Answer (a) and (b). Show your working on the lines.

parts.text: Is Ben correct? Circle Yes or No.

go.hint: The 9 is 1 less than 10. The 11 is 1 more than 10.
go.solution: 9 is 1 less than 10 and 11 is 1 more than 10, so they make up for each other: 9 + 10 + 11 = 30 = 10 + 10 + 10. In the same way 19 + 20 + 21 is three 20s, which is 60.
mistakes: Saying No because the numbers look different.

go.text: Find double 35. Fill in the missing numbers. Show your working on the lines.
go.hint: Split 35 into 30 and 5. Double each part, then put them together.
go.solution: 35 is 30 and 5. Double 30 is 60. Double 5 is 10. 60 + 10 = 70. So double 35 is 70.

investigation.title: Make two groups the same
investigation.first: Draw 6 dots and 8 dots. Move 1 dot from the 8 to the 6. What do you see? Now try 5 and 9.
investigation.text: Draw dots for 7 and 8. Can you move dots to make both groups the same? Try 6 and 8, then 5 and 9, then 7 and 8. When does it work? Write what you notice.
investigation.answer: It works for 6 and 8 (both 7), and for 5 and 9 (both 7): the two numbers are 2 apart or 4 apart and the total is a double (14). It does not work for 7 and 8: the total is 15 and one dot is always left over.
investigation.look_for: A child who tries several pairs, moves dots, and notices that when the total is a double the two groups can be made the same, and that 7 and 8 always leave one dot over. Credit any clear reason. Do not use the words odd or even yet: that is the next lesson.
mistakes: Moving too many dots across, so the groups swap instead of matching.

talk.question: Mei adds 7 + 8. She says it is 1 more than double 7. Ali says it is 1 less than double 8. Is Mei right? Is Ali right? Use counters to show.
talk.answer: Both are right. Double 7 is 14 and 1 more is 15. Double 8 is 16 and 1 less is 15. Both ways give 15, because the 8 is one more than 7 and one less than a double 8.
talk.look_for: A reason about moving one counter: one more than the smaller double, or one less than the larger double. Not just both are 15.

exit.solution: 9 + 9 = 18. Move 1 from one 9 to the other: 10 and 8.
Double 3 is 6, so double 3 tens is 6 tens: 60.
Double 8 is 16 and 1 more is 17. Or double 9 is 18 and 1 less is 17.

home_practice.text: Fill in the missing numbers. (a) Double 4 is []. (b) Double 6 is [2]. (c) Double 8 is [2].
Mei has 7 red marbles and 7 blue marbles. How many marbles does she have altogether? She has ___ marbles.
home_practice.solution: 7 + 7 = 14. Two of the same number is a double.

home_practice.text: Fill in the missing numbers. (a) Double 20 is [2]. (b) Double 40 is [2].
home_practice.solution: Double 2 tens is 4 tens: 40. Double 4 tens is 8 tens: 80.
Double 6 is 12 and 1 more is 13. Double 9 is 18 and 1 more is 19.
The 8 is 1 more than 7 and the 6 is 1 less, so the sum is five 7s: 35.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: a near double is always 1 more than the double of the smaller number. Test it with 4 + 5, 9 + 10 and 12 + 13. Does it always work?
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Test 4 + 5, 9 + 10 and 12 + 13. Is each total one more than the smaller double?
menu.answer: Yes. 4 + 5 = 9 (double 4 is 8), 9 + 10 = 19 (double 9 is 18), 12 + 13 = 25 (double 12 is 24). The bigger number is always 1 more than the smaller, so the total is 1 more than its double.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Write three near doubles, such as 6 + 7. Give them to your grown-up. Can they find each total with a double?
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Write three near doubles for a grown-up and check their answers with counters.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check that the two numbers are next to each other and that each total is right, for example 6 + 7 = 13, 8 + 9 = 17, 5 + 6 = 11.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never seen a double. Teach them how to add 7 + 8 with a double.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how to add 7 + 8 with a double.
menu.answer: Double 7 is 14. The 8 is 1 more than 7, so add 1: 15. Or double 8 is 16, take 1 away: 15.

parent.summary: We learned doubles (two of the same number, like 6 + 6 = 12) and used them to add numbers that are next to each other (6 + 7 is double 6 and 1 more). We also doubled tens (30 + 30). Doubles to 20 and a double with 1 more or 1 less are close to school Primary 1 work. Doubling a number like 35 and adding five almost-equal numbers go beyond school on purpose, in Go further only.
words: double: two of the same number added (double 6 is 6 + 6)
near double: two numbers next to each other (6 + 7)
one more, one less: the number just after or before
total: the answer when we add
try_home: Two plates: put 6 buttons on each. Say: double 6 is 12. Take 1 button away: how many now? Keep small things away from mouths.
Double it: say a number from 1 to 10. Your child says the double. Then try 20 and 30.
Near double: say 7 + 8. Ask which double helps. Then try 6 + 7 and 9 + 10.
ask: Is the total 1 more or 1 less than the double? How do you know?
Are the two numbers next to each other?
parent.when_stuck: Let your child use counters or a drawing, and wait 10 seconds before helping. Asking 'what is double the smaller number?' works better than giving the answer. If the look-back page says 'I am still stuck', photograph it and send it to our business WhatsApp (+65 9880 5962). Photos are kept 90 days after the program ends.
parent.next: Lesson 14: Odd + Odd: Always, Sometimes, Never. Online practice: your tutor will share the practice link.
parent.quote: Double, then adjust: find the double, then move one.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to use doubles to add quickly and to say why a near double is 1 more or 1 less. This week: doubles to 10 + 10, tens doubles and near doubles.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to draw a story, to use groups and sharing, and to test a claim with an example.
next_materials: 20 counters or small things of one kind (this lesson's counters are fine)
The Lesson 14 workbook, with its number cards cut out

safeguarding: Counters and small things stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Keep small things away from younger brothers and sisters.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms, so the tutor sees every camera. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.

Nobody holds paper or a board up to the camera: a gallery view shows everyone. Children tick their own work against the answer slide, answer together on a count of three, or show fingers or a thumb for a choice. There is no private chat.

Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted. Children may mute and keep their cameras off. A child's page is never shown.
Movement break: children need a little clear space, soft shoes or socks on a safe floor, no stairs and no running. A child may stay seated and move only their arms.

A child who is still stuck ticks 'I am still stuck' on the look-back page. A grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp only; photos are kept for 90 days after the program ends. The tutor then helps in the open session next lesson. No private messages to children, and no personal phones.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first, using a double each time. Check the Go further items (double 35 and the five-number sum) against the key.
Tell parents a week before: print the workbook pages and the kit page, cut out the kit page and find the things listed. Small things stay away from mouths and younger children.
Have the slides open and check the kit page is visible on screen share. Have a paper copy of the kit page and counters to show on camera if you wish.
Check the recording captures the tutor and the shared screen. Children's video is excluded; any unmuted voice is recorded. Start the recording after the greeting, and avoid first names while it runs.

Be plain with families: this lesson is flagged as a new topic and still needs the owner or a tutor syllabus check. Doubles to 20, tens doubles and near doubles sit inside the school Primary 1 idea of adding within 20 and 100. Go further goes beyond school on purpose (double 35, five numbers that are almost the same). Do not call it MOE-aligned.
